parts.title: Running a soup stall
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Two years ago I was working in an office and spent every lunchtime in the same queue for the same sandwich. I loved cooking at home, and my friends always asked me for my carrot and ginger soup. One day my neighbour, who sells flowers at the Saturday market in Lindale, suggested that I try selling it. I laughed, but a week later I was standing behind a small table with a big pot, a small cooker and forty paper cups.

I was very nervous. The first customer was a woman with a baby, and she asked me what was in the soup. I started to explain and then realised that everyone behind her in the queue was listening. By noon the pot was empty. I had never felt so tired, or so pleased.

Now I run the stall every weekend and still work in the office during the week. People often tell me I should open a proper cafe, but I am not sure. A cafe would mean staff and long hours, and I would probably spend less time cooking and more time on office work. For the moment, I prefer to keep things small. What I like best is that regular customers now tell me about their week while they drink their soup. Next month I am going to try a new soup with pumpkin, and I hope they will like it.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer start the stall?
options: She was tired of her office job.
A neighbour gave her the idea.
Her friends wanted to open a cafe.
questions.explanation: Her neighbour, who sells flowers at the market, suggested that she try selling her soup.

questions.prompt: What happened when the first customer asked about the soup?
options: Nobody wanted to buy any soup.
She forgot what was in the soup.
questions.explanation: She started to explain and then realised that everyone behind the customer was listening.

questions.prompt: Why is the writer not sure about opening a cafe?
options: She does not have enough customers.
She thinks her soup is too simple.
She would have less time to cook.
questions.explanation: She says she would probably spend less time cooking and more time on office work.

questions.prompt: What does the writer enjoy most about the stall?
options: Trying out new recipes at home.
questions.explanation: She says what she likes best is that regular customers tell her about their week.

questions.prompt: What is the writer going to do next month?
questions.explanation: She says she is going to try a new soup with pumpkin next month.

parts.title: A kitchen garden at school
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
At Lindale Primary School, the old tennis court behind the gym is no longer empty. Since March it has been a kitchen garden with ten wooden boxes full of vegetables and herbs. [1] Each class looks after one box, and the children water the plants every morning before lessons.

The idea came from the school cook, who was worried about the food that was thrown away every day. [2] She thought that if the children grew vegetables themselves, they might want to eat them.

The first months were not easy. [3] But the pupils did not give up, and in June they picked their first tomatoes.

Now the cook uses the vegetables in school lunches every Friday. [4] On those days, almost every plate comes back to the kitchen empty.

The school is already planning to build five more boxes next year. [5] The cook hopes other schools in the area will copy the idea.
sentences: Many pupils said they simply did not like vegetables.
Parents have already offered to help with the building.
Some parents grow tomatoes on their balconies at home.
The pupils chose what to grow, from carrots to mint.
Insects ate most of the lettuces, and the beans grew very slowly.
The change in the dining room has surprised everyone.

gaps.explanation: "The pupils chose what to grow" explains the vegetables and herbs in the boxes, and leads to "Each class looks after one box".
The cook was worried about wasted food because many pupils did not like vegetables; "She thought that if the children grew vegetables themselves" then gives her solution.
The first months were not easy because insects ate the lettuces and the beans grew slowly; "But the pupils did not give up" answers these problems.
"The change in the dining room has surprised everyone" introduces the surprising result in the next sentence, that almost every plate comes back empty.
Parents offering to help with the building follows the plan for five more boxes, and then "The cook hopes" gives the hope that other schools will copy the idea.

parts.title: A simple tomato soup
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: This soup is quick and cheap to make. First, [1] a little oil in a large pan until it is hot. Then fry an onion and two cloves of garlic gently for five minutes. Then add a tin of tomatoes and half a litre of water. [2] that, bring the soup to the boil. Let it cook slowly [3] twenty minutes. When the soup is ready, [4] it with salt and pepper and add a few fresh basil leaves. These amounts are [5] for four people. Any soup that is left over can be [6] in the fridge for three days.

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: Only "heat" fits "until it is hot": you heat oil in a pan until it is hot, then fry the vegetables.

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: "After that" follows the step of adding the tomatoes and water, so the soup is brought to the boil next.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: "For" is used with a length of time: cook slowly for twenty minutes.

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: To season food means to add salt and pepper to it.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: "Enough for four people" means the right amount for four people.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: Soup that is left over can be kept in the fridge for three days; taken, spent and made do not fit "in the fridge for three days".

parts.title: An invitation to dinner
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage:
Hi Blake,
Thank you [1] your message! I am so glad you can come to my dinner party on Saturday. I have invited eight people, [2] I need to cook a lot of food. I am going to make a big vegetable pie and a chocolate cake. Is there [3] you do not eat? Please let me know [4] Friday evening. I will start cooking at four o'clock, so [5] you can come early, you could help me with the salad. It will be lovely to see you, because we have not met [6] March!
Nia

gaps.explanation: We thank someone "for" something, here for the message.
"So" introduces the result: she has invited eight people, so she needs to cook a lot.
In a question, "anything" is used before "you do not eat".
"By Friday evening" means no later than Friday evening.
The condition "if you can come early" leads to the offer "you could help me".
With the present perfect "have not met", "since March" gives the starting point.

parts.title: A talk at a cooking school
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: speaker-1
turns.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to the open day at Lindale Cooking School. My name's Birgit and I'm one of the chefs here. This morning there are three short lessons in the main kitchen. The first one starts at eleven and is about making fresh pasta. At twelve there's a lesson on knife skills, where you'll learn to cut vegetables quickly and safely. The last lesson, at one o'clock, is about desserts, and you'll be able to taste everything you make. If you decide to join us, our courses last six weeks and take place on Wednesday evenings. Students need to bring their own apron, but we provide all the ingredients. Finally, everyone who signs up today will receive a free recipe book. You can ask me questions at the front desk after the lessons.

parts.title: An interview with a baker
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Minh, you run the best-known bakery in Lindale. Did you always want to be a baker?

turns.speaker: minh
turns.text: Not at all. I trained as an electrician. But I used to help my uncle in his bakery in the school holidays, and I never forgot the smell of fresh bread early in the morning. When I was twenty-six, my uncle became ill and I took over for a few weeks. In the end I stayed.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What do you find most difficult about the job these days?

turns.speaker: minh
turns.text: The hours were hard at first. I get up at three every morning so the bread is ready by seven. But I've got used to that. The difficult thing now is keeping prices fair when flour costs more every year.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Your bread is famous. Is it a secret recipe?

turns.speaker: minh
turns.text: Ha, no. Anyone can make it with flour, water and salt. The secret is time. I let the dough rest for almost twenty hours. People want to hurry, but good bread can't be hurried.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Do you teach other people?

turns.speaker: minh
turns.text: I run a children's class on the first Saturday of every month. The children make little rolls and take them home. It's noisy and there's flour everywhere, but it's the part of the month I enjoy most.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Have you ever made a big mistake?

turns.speaker: minh
turns.text: Yes! One winter I forgot about forty loaves in the oven. They came out as hard as stones. I gave everybody a new loaf the next day, free of charge, and now I set two alarms.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: And what are your plans for the future?

turns.speaker: minh
turns.text: I'd love to open a small cafe next to the bakery, but my wife says we need a holiday first. So the next step is a week in Portugal!

questions.prompt: How did Minh become a baker?

He answered an advert in the paper.
questions.explanation: He had trained as an electrician, but when his uncle became ill he took over the bakery and stayed.

questions.prompt: What does Minh find most difficult these days?
questions.explanation: He has got used to the hours; the difficult thing now is keeping prices fair as flour costs more.

questions.explanation: The recipe is not secret; the secret is time, because the dough rests for almost twenty hours.

questions.explanation: The class is noisy, but he says it is the part of the month he enjoys most.

questions.explanation: He gave everybody a new loaf the next day, free of charge.
